newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PG&E battles government on pipe plan.
newsitem.headline: PG&E battles government on pipe plan.

text.p: U.S. energy giant Pacific Gas & Electric Corp plans to press ahead with its proposed A$1 billion Dampier-Bunbury natural gas pipeline in Western Australia despite opposition from the state government, a company spokeswoman told Reuters on Monday.

PG&E subsidiary PGT Australia hopes the cool reception it received from the government to its proposal over the weekend would not halt the development, which is in the best interests of Western Australia, Meg McKnight, public affairs manager for PGT Australia, told Reuters.
Government approval was needed in six to nine months if the pipeline were to begin operation in 2000 as planned, she said.

McKnight rejected weekend statements by Western Australia Mines and Energy Minister Colin Barnett that the PGT plan was aimed at reducing the value of the Dampier-Bunbury pipeline of state-owned utility AlintaGas.
Barnett, who was in cabinet on Monday and unavailable for comment, has said a second line could wipe up to A$300 million off the value of the existing line.
At the weekend he described the PGT proposal as provocative and aimed at pre-empting state energy policy.

A government spokesperson stressed to Reuters on Monday that PGT Australia was not the first company to express interest in building a second Dampier to Bunbury pipeline. "(The PGT proposal) still requires government approval and other companies are interested in such a pipeline," the spokesperson said.
The government plans to partly privatise the existing Dampier to Bunbury pipeline through the sale of a half interest.
This pipeline was valued at A$1.2 billion but carried A$900 million in debt underwritten by the government, Barnett said.
McKnight said the AlintaGas pipeline was at capacity and additional needs had been identified.
New customers were coming on stream, with Kingstream Resources NL's proposed A$1.4 billion steel plant at Geraldton one important potential customer, McKnight said.

Kingstream has called for tenders for the supply of gas at rates of up to 170 terajoules (tJ) a day to its Geraldton steel project, which is scheduled to begin production at 2.4 million tonnes of steel slab a year in year 2000.
McKnight said PGT was the most competitive bidder to supply Kingstream but would not speculate on how firm Kingstream was as a potential customer for PGT pipeline gas.
The PGT pipeline represented an important opportunity for Western Australia, she said.
PGT, which has lodged an application with the state government for development of the pipeline, would continue to work with potential customers and suppliers, she added.
